sources.title: Cuneiform tablet: administrative account concerning the distribution of barley and emmer
notes: Proto-cuneiform appeared in southern Mesopotamia at the end of the fourth millennium BCE.
Early tablets recorded economic information such as deliveries and distributions of grain.
Pictograms were pressed into clay with a stylus and gradually developed into wedge-shaped cuneiform.
sources.apa: The Metropolitan Museum of Art. (n.d.). Cuneiform tablet: administrative account concerning the distribution of barley and emmer. https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/327384
sources.citation: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, n.d.

sources.title: From Accounting to Writing
sources.publisher: University of Texas at Austin, Denise Schmandt-Besserat
sources.reliability: University research page by an archaeologist
notes: Clay tokens were used in accounting systems to track goods such as grain and livestock.
The relationship between tokens, seals and writing is a scholarly reconstruction, not a single proven linear path.
Administrative signs eventually developed into ways of recording language and names.
sources.apa: University of Texas at Austin, Denise Schmandt-Besserat. (n.d.). From Accounting to Writing. https://sites.utexas.edu/dsb/tokens/from-accounting-to-writing/
sources.citation: University of Texas at Austin, Denise Schmandt-Besserat, n.d.

sources.title: Origins of Writing: Support notes for tutors
notes: Writing systems were created independently in multiple regions of the world.
Early writing was useful for taxes, contracts, rations and administration.
Literacy was restricted to a relatively small group in many ancient societies.
sources.apa: The British Museum. (n.d.). Origins of Writing: Support notes for tutors. https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/2019-11/Origins-of-writing-support-notes-for-teachers_final.pdf

sources.title: 3.2 Ancient Mesopotamia
notes: The earliest known evidence of writing includes cuneiform from Sumer around 3000 BCE or earlier.
Researchers have proposed that clay tokens and accounting practices preceded writing.
The exact pathway from accounting marks to a writing system remains a subject of historical interpretation.

sources.title: Cuneiform tablets
sources.publisher: Museum of Classical Antiquities, University of Ottawa
notes: Cuneiform was pressed into fresh clay using a wedge-shaped tool.
Early tablets commonly had practical accounting purposes.
Cuneiform was later adapted to record multiple languages.
sources.apa: Museum of Classical Antiquities, University of Ottawa. (n.d.). Cuneiform tablets. https://omeka.uottawa.ca/museumclassicalantiquities/exhibits/show/writing-and-languages/cuneiform
